title: Predictive control of plant cell-division planes and tissue patterning

concept.text: The innovation would make it possible to predict where and in which orientation a plant cell will divide, then deliberately redirect that division to produce a specified tissue pattern. Its central task is to connect cell geometry and mechanical stress with the molecular processes that specify a division site and guide the phragmoplast, the cellular apparatus involved in positioning the new partition between daughter cells.

As a synthesis of the supplied research and review, the intended capability extends from predicting an individual division to explaining the tissue pattern that follows a controlled intervention. It would accommodate differences among species, tissues and cell types, including variation in the mechanisms used and the accuracy of division placement. Success would therefore require a model that identifies its operating conditions and uncertainty, rather than assuming identical machinery or perfectly positioned divisions everywhere.

significance.text: If achieved, prospective prediction and causal redirection of division planes across tissues would provide a substantial new capability for understanding plant body formation. Researchers could test whether a proposed relationship among geometry, forces and division machinery actually determines a division outcome, and whether changing that outcome produces the expected tissue pattern. The advance would be especially consequential if it transferred across biological contexts instead of requiring a separate explanation for each experimental system.

Conditional downstream possibilities include directing aspects of organ shape through controlled tissue patterning. This is a proposed impact, not an established consequence: division orientation alone does not determine whole-organ architecture. Producing a designed organ would require coordinated control of additional developmental processes, including growth and cell identity, and evidence that the intended pattern persists as development proceeds. Predictive control of division placement would therefore be an enabling capability rather than a complete method for designing plant form.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is an experimentally validated connection from a cell's starting geometry and mechanical environment through division-site selection and execution to the resulting tissue arrangement. The supplied research identifies several parts of this chain, but does not establish an integrated predictive and controllable system. A key distinction is between selecting a prospective division site and successfully guiding the later partition to that site: explaining one step would not by itself explain the other.

As a synthesis of the research target, concrete barriers include determining how geometric and mechanical inputs are combined, how an early spatial specification is retained during division, and how the later guidance machinery uses that information. A useful account must also explain variation and errors: when placement remains reliable despite perturbation, when it changes, and whether different cell types achieve similar outcomes through different mechanisms. The supplied materials do not resolve these questions or establish which remain open in current research.

A further engineering challenge is to make a chosen intervention produce a predictable tissue outcome. Manipulating a force or molecular component must be linked to a specified change in division placement, with enough measurement and experimental control to distinguish that effect from other changes in cell behavior. Transfer across species and tissues would require identifying which relationships generalize, which parameters need recalibration, and where a different model is necessary. These are proposed requirements for the innovation, not capabilities demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies Pantelis Livanos and Sabine Müller's review, “Division Plane Establishment and Cytokinesis,” as first published on 22 February 2019, with DOI 10.1146/annurev-arplant-050718-100444. It attributes to that review an account in which the preprophase band transiently marks the division site while other proteins persist as spatial references and guide the phragmoplast. This provides a specific historical attribution for the proposed distinction between early site marking and later guidance; it is not independently verified document content in the supplied evidence package.

The earlier research reports that the abstract and article reference annotations were accessible but that the full-text display did not load. The subsequent review had no saved source text or retained document artifact with which to check either the biological account or that access report. Accordingly, the material cannot support a detailed reconstruction of the review's experiments, their quantitative performance, their biological scope or the precise wording and scope of its open questions. This limitation does not establish that the attributed account is false.

The earlier research also describes unresolved questions about division-site selection and robustness. Whether those questions remained open as of the review's 1 November 2026 freshness cutoff is unresolved: no subsequent evidence or freshness-search results were supplied. The package therefore does not establish either completion of the proposed cross-species predictive-control capability or its present-day absence. It supplies no verified prediction accuracies, intervention effect sizes, rescue results or cross-species demonstrations from which to assess progress toward that capability.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: make prospective predictions of division orientation and placement in multiple cell types, tissues and species, then compare them with observed divisions. Before testing, specify the predicted outcomes, allowable spatial and angular errors, treatment of uncertainty, and comparisons with simpler geometric predictions. Report failures and context-dependent performance as well as successes. These are proposed evaluation choices, not established field standards; the supplied material provides no basis for selecting numerical thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective division-plane predictions match observed divisions across biological contexts

completion_criteria.text: Proposed causal demonstration: manipulate specified molecular components or mechanical conditions, predict the resulting change in division placement, and show that the change occurs reproducibly. Where feasible, restoring the perturbed component or condition should rescue the predicted behavior. Prediction tests explanatory power, intervention tests causality, and rescue strengthens the interpretation that the intended mechanism produced the effect. The experiments should also connect altered divisions to measured tissue-pattern outcomes rather than treating orientation changes alone as completion.
completion_criteria.label: Interventions reproduce predicted division-placement changes with measured tissue-pattern outcomes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat the results across independent experiments and, ideally, independent laboratories, with documented measurement methods and accessible data and analysis. Define the biological contexts, intervention timing and magnitude over which control works, and assess whether the resulting tissue develops as intended. For any organ-shaping application, demonstrate the organ outcome separately. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth and known limits, not literal universality across plants or proof that every cell uses the same mechanism.
completion_criteria.label: Independent experiments reproduce division control with documented practical biological limits

related_concepts.text: BOT-13, “A predictive mechanism for plant cell-wall growth and mechanical sensing,” is the closest proposed overlap: forces and mechanical responses could connect cell-wall behavior with division orientation. The distinction is the outcome being explained and controlled. BOT-13 concerns growth and mechanical sensing, whereas BOT-17 concerns division-site specification, execution and resulting tissue patterns. This comparison is inferred from the roster title and the supplied research's overlap statement; BOT-13's detailed record was not provided.

BOT-05, “Predictive plant biology from genome to whole-organism performance,” has a broader predictive scope. Based on the roster titles, a validated account of division placement could contribute a developmental component to that larger goal, but predicting cell divisions would not by itself predict whole-organism performance. Conversely, a successful whole-plant predictor would not necessarily provide causal control of division sites. The two entries retain distinct completion targets.

BOT-03, “Whole-plant synthetic genome construction and rewriting,” and BOT-04, “An inexpensive, broadly transferable method to edit and regenerate plants,” concern potentially complementary ways to construct or modify plants. As a title-based synthesis, those capabilities might help implement molecular interventions used by BOT-17, but the ability to edit or rewrite a genome would not establish how an intervention changes division geometry or tissue pattern. BOT-17's distinctive requirement remains prospective prediction coupled to reproducible causal control.

The earlier report of accessible abstract and reference annotations, and an unavailable full-text display, cannot be independently checked from the supplied package.

brief.title: Predicting and steering how plant cells divide
possible: Researchers could predict where a plant cell will form the wall separating its daughters, then redirect that wall to create a chosen arrangement of cells. The predictions would account for differences among species, tissues and cell types.
why: This would let researchers test how cell shape, physical forces and molecular machinery work together to build plant tissues. Connecting a deliberate change in division to the resulting tissue pattern would help explain how plants acquire their form.

sources.showed: This review describes how plant cells mark a future division site and guide the new dividing wall toward it.
sources.cited_for: It supports the distinction between choosing a division site and guiding the new wall to that site.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a system for predicting and redirecting divisions to produce chosen tissue patterns.

sources.showed: In roots of the plant Arabidopsis, stretching stabilized microtubules, internal supporting fibres. Their rearrangement changed the orientation of cell divisions during wound healing.
sources.quote:
Microtubules are destabilized under
low tension, whereas stretching of cells, either through wounding or external aspiration, immediately induces
their polymerization.
sources.cited_for: It links mechanical forces to molecular changes and redirected divisions during root repair.
sources.not_established: Root wound healing does not establish reliable control of chosen tissue patterns across species and tissues.

sources.showed: In the outer layer of Arabidopsis roots, actin, another internal supporting fibre, helped cells divide in directions that cell shape alone would not predict.
sources.quote: we show that actin is a central molecular actor required to establish cell division orientation against the geometrical rules, highlighting its role in integrating spatial information.
sources.cited_for: It identifies a molecular component that helps division orientation override predictions based on cell shape.
sources.not_established: Identifying actin’s role does not establish how to choose and reliably produce a desired tissue arrangement.

shown: Hoermayer and colleagues connected stretching, supporting fibres and redirected divisions during root repair. Goldy and colleagues showed that a different supporting fibre helps root cells override the division direction predicted by their shape. These results identify parts of the control system in particular root tissues.
missing: A tested model must connect starting cell shape and forces to division-site selection, wall placement and the resulting tissue pattern.
Chosen interventions must reliably produce predicted changes in division placement and measured tissue arrangements.
Control must work across biological contexts, with clear limits on where and when it succeeds.

milestones.label: Predicted divisions match outcomes across species and tissues
milestones.explanation: Predictions made before division would have to match observed wall positions and orientations across biological contexts, with stated error limits. This would test whether the model travels beyond a particular tissue.

milestones.label: Interventions produce predicted divisions and tissue patterns
milestones.explanation: Changes to forces or molecular components would have to reproducibly cause predicted wall placements and measured tissue patterns. Restoring the original conditions where feasible would strengthen the causal explanation.

milestones.label: Independent experiments reproduce control and establish its limits
milestones.explanation: Independent experiments would have to reproduce control and establish its biological limits, including how tissue develops afterward. Any proposed organ-shaping use would need a separate demonstration of the organ outcome.

uncertain: How cells combine shape, forces and molecular signals to select a division site remains unclear.
Different cell types may reach similar division outcomes through different mechanisms.
Acceptable prediction errors, biological coverage and tissue-pattern outcomes still need to be defined.

page.title: Predictive control of plant cell division planes
page.definition: A model predicts where a plant cell will build the wall separating its daughters and selects an intervention that redirects that wall to produce a specified tissue pattern. The model connects cell geometry and forces to division-site selection and the machinery that builds and guides the wall.

goal.need: Root divisions can add cells within an existing cell file or create new files, with different consequences for tissue architecture. In three cell populations, a minimum-area geometric rule matched 66–91% of observed divisions, with 289–545 cells sampled per population. Predictive control would connect these geometric regularities and their departures to interventions that produce specified cell arrangements.

figures.caption: Agreement with the global minimum-area rule, reported on 7 March 2011.
figures.note: These are observed frequencies, not prospective prediction accuracies or accepted performance thresholds.

statements.body: Plant Science Decadal Vision committee, convened by the American Society of Plant Biologists
statements.quote: Increase the ability to predict plant traits from plant genomes in diverse environments
statements.context: This broader plant-science objective encompasses predictive development but does not specify division-plane performance.

statements.body: European Research Council-funded COMPASS programme, coordinated by CNRS
statements.quote: In walled organisms such as plants, the division plane's position irreversibly defines tissue topology and is tightly controlled.
statements.context: Tissue topology describes which cells are neighbours.

completion.title: A model-selected intervention produces a specified plant tissue pattern through redirected cell divisions.
completion.criterion: A model uses initial cell geometry and mechanical and molecular conditions to select an intervention for a cell-neighbour arrangement specified before treatment in a defined living plant tissue. After the selected cells complete division, imaging shows the predicted new-wall orientations and the specified pattern of which daughter cells touch which neighbours. The test covers the declared tissue and intervention only. No external numerical accuracy or replication threshold was found.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body was found to have defined an integrated prediction-and-control acceptance test.
completion.basis: Searches of ERC TORPEDO and COMPASS objectives, plant-science decadal visions, and division-plane benchmark and protocol literature found no integrated acceptance test. The fallback combines division-orientation control with the tissue-topology objective in one tissue. The 2019 review distinguishes spatial marking from subsequent wall guidance, supporting assessment of completed walls.

milestones.title: An observed plant division matches the minimum-area wall separating equal-volume daughters.
milestones.criterion: For a symmetric division, the observed new wall has the minimum-area geometry that partitions the mother cell into equal-volume daughters. This is the Errera–Sachs geometric benchmark. Besson and Dumais demonstrated agreement for subsets of the populations tabulated above, while documenting alternative division planes. Agreement with this benchmark does not establish causal control or universal prediction.
milestones.set_by: Errera's and Sachs's rules, as formulated and experimentally examined by Besson and Dumais in 2011; a geometric convention for symmetric divisions.
milestones.threshold_quote: In the case of symmetric cell division, the plane of least area is selected such that it creates two daughter cells of equal size

milestones.title: A genetic screen identifies components that convert division triggers into changed division orientation.
milestones.criterion: An unbiased genetic screen identifies downstream components that translate an established periclinal-division trigger into changed division orientation. Periclinal divisions form walls parallel to the tissue surface and add cell files. TORPEDO's report covering 1 August 2021 to 31 July 2022 records resistant and hypersensitive mutants and mapped causal mutations. The report supplies no sample sizes; this reported result is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: European Research Council-funded TORPEDO programme, objective 2 in its published grant description; written for induced periclinal divisions.
milestones.threshold_quote: Identifying novel downstream components that translate the known genetic triggers for PD into changes in cell division orientation by performing an unbiased genetic screen.

milestones.title: A model-selected intervention produces a prospectively specified daughter-cell wall in living plant tissue.
milestones.criterion: The model selects an intervention that produces the specified completed wall. Supporting results remain narrower: Hoermayer et al. linked wound-driven redirection to microtubule orientation in one illustrated Arabidopsis root ablation on 4 April 2024. Goldy et al., published on 18 February 2026, reconstructed 10 cells per epidermal cell type and condition and simulated 500 divisions per cell; actin perturbation shifted divisions toward geometric predictions. Neither paper reports this prospective intervention-selection test.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of the ERC objectives and division-plane prediction and perturbation literature found no acceptance criterion for model-selected wall placement.

not_found: No external integrated completion criterion, prediction-error tolerance or required biological coverage was found in the programme objectives, decadal visions or benchmark searches.
No published demonstration was found of a model selecting division-plane interventions to produce a prospectively specified tissue cell-neighbour pattern.
The opened 2019 review page provided its abstract and bibliography but did not display the full text.

results.finding: In one illustrated Arabidopsis root ablation, cells with longitudinal/transversal microtubule ratios above 1.0 changed division orientation.
results.detail: The illustrated ablation links microtubule orientation to division-plane changes. The paper does not report a model selecting an intervention to produce a prospectively specified wall.
results.quote:
Cells with longitudinal/transversal ratios of above 1.0
changed division planes from anticlinal (transversal) to periclinal
(longitudinal), whereas cells with ratios below 1.0 maintained
the normally occurring, anticlinal (transversal) division planes.

results.finding: In 10 wild-type atrichoblasts, observed divisions aligned with predicted minimal area; relative interface area was approximately 0.
results.detail: The comparison used near-symmetric simulated divisions with daughter-volume ratios above 0.42 and sampled local minima. It does not establish an exactly equal-volume, globally minimum-area wall.
results.quote: In atrichoblast (A), the observed division planes were oriented following the model’s predicted minimal surface area (relative interface ~0).

results.finding: After actin perturbation, root epidermal divisions followed geometric predictions; 10 cells per type and condition were reconstructed.
results.detail: The study simulated 500 divisions per reconstructed cell and observed shifts after actin perturbation. It did not use the model to select an intervention for a prospectively specified completed wall.
results.quote:
Yet, when we simulated cell divisions in both trichoblast and atrichoblast in WT after LatB or in the
act7-4
, all the epidermal cells followed geometrical rule to divide

results.finding: A genetic screen identified one SPK1 loss-of-function allele associated with reduced periclinal divisions; sample size not reported.
results.detail: The paper links PEAR-promoted division orientation to ROPGEF–ROP signaling, but the supplied text does not establish that the screen was unbiased or that SPK1 was identified as a downstream component of the PEAR trigger. The screen’s parental line was not induced in the reported mutant comparison.
results.quote:
Therefore, we focused on the loss-of-function alleles of
SPK1
, one of which we identified in the genetic screen for factors promoting formative (periclinal) cell divisions (
Supplementary Materials
).
